message.content:
### Short answer **It depends on what you’re trying to do.** If you need fast, in‑memory lookups and you’re already using Python, a *dictionary of Pandas Series* (or a single `DataFrame` with a `MultiIndex`) is usually the most convenient. If you’re storing millions of points on disk and need efficient range queries, a *time‑series database* (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, VictoriaMetrics, etc.) or a *columnar store* (Parquet + DuckDB) is the way to go. If you’re building a distributed cache or need sub‑millisecond latency, a *Redis sorted set* or a *Cassandra table with a composite key* works well. Below is a quick‑reference cheat sheet that covers the most common patterns, their trade‑offs, and when you’d pick each one. --- ## 1. In‑memory, Python‑centric | Structure | Typical API | Pros | Cons | When to use | |-----------|-------------|------|------|--------------| | **`dict[str, dict[datetime, float]]`**
e.g. `{ 'USD/EUR': { ts1: val1, ts2: val2 } }` | `data[currency][ts]` | • Very fast O(1) lookup
• Simple to serialize (JSON, pickle)
• No external dependencies | • Memory‑heavy for large datasets
• No built‑in range queries | • Small to medium data (< 10 M points)
• Quick prototyping | | **`dict[str, pandas.Series]`**
e.g. `{ 'USD/EUR': pd.Series(vals, index=ts) }` | `data[currency].loc[ts]` | • Built‑in resampling, interpolation, rolling windows
• Index is `DatetimeIndex` → fast slicing
• Works with NumPy & SciPy | • Still memory‑heavy
• Requires Pandas | • Analytics / ML pipelines
• Need vectorized ops | | **`pandas.DataFrame` with `MultiIndex`**
e.g. `df.index = pd.MultiIndex.from_product([ts, currencies])` | `df.loc[(ts, currency)]` | • One object, easy to export to CSV/Parquet
• Groupby / pivot tables trivial
• Can be sliced by time or currency | • Indexing can be slower than dict
• Requires Pandas | • One‑stop shop for reporting & ad‑hoc queries | ### Quick code snippets ```python import pandas as pd from datetime import datetime # 1. Dict of Series ts = pd.date_range('2024-01-01', periods=5, freq='D') vals = [1.1, 1.2, 1.15, 1.18, 1.22] series = pd.Series(vals, index=ts) data = {'USD/EUR': series} # 2. DataFrame with MultiIndex df = pd.DataFrame({'value': vals}, index=ts) df['currency'] = 'USD/EUR' df = df.set_index(['currency', df.index]) ``` --- ## 2. On‑disk, relational style | Table | Columns | Indexes | Pros | Cons | When to use | |-------|---------|---------|------|------|--------------| | **`currency_rates`** | `currency_code TEXT`, `ts TIMESTAMP`, `rate NUMERIC` | Composite PK (`currency_code`, `ts`) | • SQL tooling (PostgreSQL, SQLite)
• ACID guarantees
• Easy joins | • Range queries can be slow without proper indexes
• Requires a DBMS | • Small to medium data (< 100 M rows)
• Need transactional consistency | | **`currency_rates_tsdb`** | Same columns | Time‑partitioned index | • Fast range scans
• Compression | • Requires TSDB (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB) | • High‑frequency data (ticks, OHLCV) | ### Example schema (PostgreSQL) ```sql CREATE TABLE currency_rates ( currency_code TEXT NOT NULL, ts TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, rate NUMERIC NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (currency_code, ts) ); -- Optional: create a separate index for range queries CREATE INDEX idx_currency_ts ON currency_rates (currency_code, ts); ``` --- ## 3. Columnar / analytical stores | Format | Tool | Pros | Cons | When to use | |--------|------|------|------|--------------| | **Parquet** | `pyarrow`, `pandas`, `duckdb` | • Columnar compression
• Efficient for read‑only analytics
• Works with big‑data frameworks | • Write‑heavy workloads are slower
• No ACID | • Batch analytics
• Data lake ingestion | | **DuckDB** | In‑process SQL engine | • Zero‑config, fast on local files
• Supports window functions, joins | • Not a full‑blown DBMS | • Interactive analytics on Parquet | --- ## 4. Distributed / low‑latency caches | Store | Key | Value | Pros | Cons | When to use | |-------|-----|-------|------|------|--------------| | **Redis Sorted Set** | `currency:ts` | `rate` | • O(log N) insert & range query
• In‑memory, sub‑ms latency | • Limited to RAM
• No persistence unless configured | • Real‑time dashboards
• Rate‑limit / sliding window | | **Cassandra** | Composite key (`currency`, `ts`) | `rate` | • Linear scalability
• Tunable consistency | • Writes are eventually consistent
• Requires cluster | • High write throughput
• Geo‑distributed deployments | --- ## 5. Hybrid / “best of both worlds” | Pattern | How it works | Pros | Cons | When to use | |---------|--------------|------|------|--------------| | **Cache + DB** | Keep hot data in Redis, archive older data in PostgreSQL | • Fast reads for recent data
• Durable storage for history | • Two systems to maintain | • Trading platforms, FX desks | | **In‑memory + Parquet** | Load recent data into Pandas, dump older data to Parquet | • Fast analytics on recent data
• Cost‑effective long‑term storage | • Requires periodic sync | • Data science pipelines | --- ## 6. Choosing the right structure | Decision factor | Recommended structure | |-----------------|-----------------------| | **Data size** | < 10 M points → `dict` or `Series`
10 M–100 M → `DataFrame` or relational DB
> 100 M → TSDB or distributed store | | **Read pattern** | Point lookups → `dict`/`Series`
Range scans → TSDB / Parquet | | **Write pattern** | Low write → relational DB
High write → TSDB / Redis | | **Latency requirement** | < 1 ms → Redis / in‑memory
10–100 ms → TSDB | | **Analytics needs** | Heavy analytics → Pandas / Parquet
Light analytics → `Series` | | **Persistence** | Must persist → DB / Parquet
Optional → Redis | | **Scalability** | Single node → Pandas / SQLite
Cluster → TimescaleDB / Cassandra | --- ## 7. Quick “starter” recommendation If you’re just starting out and you’re comfortable with Python: 1. **For prototyping / small data** ```python data = { 'USD/EUR': pd.Series( [1.1, 1.2, 1.15, 1.18, 1.22], index=pd.date_range('2024-01-01', periods=5, freq='D') ) } ``` 2. **For production / larger data** - Store raw data in **TimescaleDB** (PostgreSQL + hypertables). - Keep a **Redis cache** for the last 24 h of data. - Export older data to **Parquet** for long‑term analytics. --- ## 8. TL;DR cheat sheet | Use case | Best structure | Why | |----------|----------------|-----| | **Fast point lookup** | `dict[str, Series]` | O(1) hash lookup | | **Range query (last N days)** | `Series` + `.loc[start:end]` | Vectorized slicing | | **Batch analytics** | `DataFrame` + `groupby` | Pandas excels at groupby | | **High‑frequency writes** | TimescaleDB hypertable | Handles millions of inserts per second | | **Real‑time dashboard** | Redis sorted set | Sub‑ms latency | | **Long‑term storage** | Parquet + DuckDB | Columnar compression + fast reads | --- ### Final thought There’s no one‑size‑fits‑all “best” data structure. Pick the one that matches your **volume**, **access patterns**, **latency requirements**, and **operational constraints**. In practice, most teams end up using a *hybrid stack*: an in‑memory cache for hot data, a TSDB for recent history, and a columnar store for archival analytics.
